# Introduction and problem

Earthquakes are among the most damaging natural hazards. How much damage an event can cause depends mainly on its **magnitude** (energy released), its **depth** (shallow events shake the surface harder) and its **location**. A raw catalogue of tens of thousands of events is hard to read, so this case study turns a public catalogue of significant earthquakes into a clear picture of global seismic activity and ranks events by a simple, explainable severity score. The score and models describe *recorded* events; they are not a forecast and ignore population, buildings and local geology.

# Objectives

1. Clean the catalogue and describe the distribution of magnitude and depth, and the temporal and geographic patterns of earthquakes.
2. Build a transparent 0--100 **risk score** and four risk levels (Low, Moderate, High, Severe), and group earthquakes with K-means clustering.
3. **Predict** whether an event is High/Severe from location, time and catalogue information, and compare three models.

# Dataset

```{r data-load}
raw <- read_csv(P("data", "raw", "database.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE,
                col_types = cols(Date = col_character(), Time = col_character()))
```

**Source:** *Significant Earthquakes, 1965--2016* (USGS earthquake database, distributed on Kaggle: kaggle.com/datasets/usgs/earthquake-database; original catalogue at earthquake.usgs.gov). The file is in the project repository (github.com/chaithanyakumarreddy57-spec/Global-Earthquake-Risk-Analytics) as `data/raw/database.csv`.

**Size:** `r format(nrow(raw), big.mark = ",")` rows and `r ncol(raw)` columns, covering earthquakes of magnitude `r min(raw$Magnitude)` to `r max(raw$Magnitude)` from 1965 to 2016. **Important variables:** `Date`, `Time`, `Latitude`, `Longitude`, `Depth` (km), `Magnitude`, `Magnitude Type`, `Type` (earthquake, nuclear explosion, explosion, rock burst) and `Status` (automatic or reviewed).

**Why it is suitable:** it is a real, global, well-documented catalogue with exactly the variables a severity analysis needs (where, when, how large, how deep), enough records for clustering and machine learning, and mostly complete core columns (no missing values in date, location, depth or magnitude).

# Data preparation

The code below runs when the report is knitted. It follows the cleaning steps of `earthquake_analysis.R` (Phases 3, 4 and 7) and ends with a check against the saved clean dataset.

```{r prep, echo = TRUE}
eq <- raw
# snake_case names (the full script uses janitor::clean_names(), same result)
names(eq) <- tolower(gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_", names(eq)))

# 1. Duplicates: none found, distinct() is a safeguard
n_dup <- sum(duplicated(eq));  eq <- distinct(eq)

# 2. Missing values: drop columns with > 60% missing, then fill the rest
miss_pct <- colMeans(is.na(eq)) * 100
dropped  <- names(eq)[miss_pct > 60]
eq <- eq[, miss_pct <= 60]
eq$magnitude_type[is.na(eq$magnitude_type)] <- "Unknown"
eq$root_mean_square[is.na(eq$root_mean_square)] <- median(eq$root_mean_square, na.rm = TRUE)

# 3. Incorrect values: keep natural earthquakes only, depth >= 0, valid coordinates
n_before <- nrow(eq)
eq <- eq %>%
  filter(type == "Earthquake") %>%
  mutate(depth = pmax(depth, 0)) %>%                    # 3 depths were slightly negative
  filter(between(latitude, -90, 90), between(longitude, -180, 180))

# 4. Data types: 3 rows hold ISO timestamps, the rest are MM/DD/YYYY + HH:MM:SS
iso <- str_detect(eq$date, "T")
eq$datetime <- as.POSIXct(NA, tz = "UTC")
eq$datetime[iso]  <- ymd_hms(eq$date[iso], tz = "UTC")
eq$datetime[!iso] <- mdy_hms(paste(eq$date[!iso], eq$time[!iso]), tz = "UTC")

# 5. Transformations: time parts and categories
eq <- eq %>% mutate(
  year = year(datetime), month = month(datetime), hour = hour(datetime),
  depth_category = cut(depth, c(-Inf, 70, 300, Inf), right = FALSE,
                       labels = c("Shallow", "Intermediate", "Deep")))

# 6. Risk score (0-100): 60% magnitude energy + 40% shallowness (depth capped at 300 km)
mag_norm   <- (eq$magnitude - 5.5) / (max(eq$magnitude) - 5.5)
depth_norm <- 1 - pmin(eq$depth, 300) / 300
eq$risk_score <- round(100 * (0.6 * mag_norm + 0.4 * depth_norm), 2)
eq$risk_level <- cut(eq$risk_score, c(-Inf, 30, 42, 55, Inf),
                     labels = c("Low", "Moderate", "High", "Severe"))
```

```{r prep-check}
saved <- readRDS(P("data", "processed", "earthquakes_clean.rds"))
ok <- nrow(eq) == nrow(saved) &&
  isTRUE(all.equal(eq$risk_score, saved$risk_score)) &&
  all(as.character(eq$risk_level) == as.character(saved$risk_level))
stopifnot(ok)                      # the report stops if it ever disagrees with the saved data
n_removed <- n_before - nrow(eq)
nonq <- raw %>% count(Type) %>% filter(Type != "Earthquake")
```

**Result.** `r n_dup` duplicate rows were found; `r length(dropped)` columns with more than 60% missing values were dropped (`r paste(dropped, collapse = ", ")`); `r n_removed` non-earthquake records (`r paste(nonq$n, tolower(nonq$Type), collapse = ", ")`) were removed. The cleaned dataset has **`r format(nrow(eq), big.mark = ",")` earthquakes**. The check above confirms that the rows and risk scores computed here are identical to the saved file `data/processed/earthquakes_clean.rds` used by every other part of the project.

# Data analysis and visualization

## Magnitude, depth and time

```{r fig-md, echo = TRUE, fig.height = 2.5, fig.cap = "Distribution of magnitude (left) and depth (right)."}
p1 <- ggplot(eq, aes(magnitude)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, fill = "firebrick", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "Magnitude distribution", x = "Magnitude", y = "Number of earthquakes")
p2 <- ggplot(eq, aes(depth)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "Depth distribution", x = "Depth (km)", y = "Number of earthquakes")
p1 + p2 & theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```

Magnitudes are strongly right-skewed: the median is `r f2(median(eq$magnitude))` and only `r pct(mean(eq$magnitude >= 7))` of events reach magnitude 7 or more (`r sum(eq$magnitude >= 8)` reach 8 or more). Most earthquakes are shallow: `r pct(mean(eq$depth < 70))` occur above 70 km (median depth `r median(eq$depth)` km), and a small group lies deeper than 300 km. Magnitude and depth are almost uncorrelated (Spearman $\rho$ = `r f3(cor(eq$magnitude, eq$depth, method = "spearman"))`), so both are needed in the risk score.

```{r fig-year, echo = TRUE, fig.height = 2.3, fig.cap = "Number of earthquakes per year, 1965-2016."}
yearly <- count(eq, year)
ggplot(yearly, aes(year, n)) +
  geom_line(colour = "firebrick") + geom_point(size = 1) +
  labs(title = "Earthquakes per year", x = "Year", y = "Number of earthquakes") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
```

```{r trend}
tr <- summary(lm(n ~ year, yearly))$coefficients["year", ]
busiest <- yearly %>% arrange(desc(n)) %>% slice(1)
```

The yearly count rises by about `r f2(tr[1])` events per year (p `r ifelse(tr[4] < 0.001, "< 0.001", paste("=", f3(tr[4])))`). This is probably influenced by improving detection and reporting rather than a real rise in activity. The busiest year is `r busiest$year` (`r busiest$n` events), when the magnitude 9.1 Tohoku earthquake in Japan and its aftershocks occurred.

## Geographic distribution and risk levels

```{r risk-tbl}
rt <- eq %>% count(risk_level) %>%
  mutate(Share = pct(n / sum(n)),
         `Mean magnitude` = round(tapply(eq$magnitude, eq$risk_level, mean), 2),
         `Mean depth (km)` = round(tapply(eq$depth, eq$risk_level, mean), 1)) %>%
  rename(`Risk level` = risk_level, Earthquakes = n) %>%
  mutate(Earthquakes = comma(Earthquakes))
kable(rt, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = FALSE, linesep = rep("", 5),
      caption = "Earthquakes by risk level (Low: score up to 30; Moderate: to 42; High: to 55; Severe: above 55).") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 8.5)
```

```{r f-map, out.width = "88%", fig.cap = "Epicentres coloured by risk level (Severe events drawn on top)."}
include_graphics(fig("67_risk_map.png"))
```

Earthquakes follow the plate boundaries: the Pacific "Ring of Fire", the Alpine--Himalayan belt and the mid-ocean ridges. Moderate is the largest level (`r pct(mean(eq$risk_level == "Moderate"))`); `r pct(mean(eq$risk_level %in% c("High", "Severe")))` of events are High or Severe, and these concentrate along the subduction zones of the western Pacific and the South American coast. Low-risk events are all deeper than 70 km, because shallowness is part of the score. The most active 10$^\circ$ x 10$^\circ$ cell (20$^\circ$S--10$^\circ$S, 160$^\circ$E--170$^\circ$E, near Vanuatu) holds `r comma(read_csv(P("outputs","tables","grid_cells.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)$n[1])` events.

## Clustering

```{r cl}
cl <- read_csv(P("outputs", "tables", "cluster_profile.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
cl %>% transmute(Cluster = cluster, Earthquakes = comma(n), `Mean magnitude` = round(mean_mag, 2),
                 `Mean depth (km)` = round(mean_depth, 1), `Mean risk score` = round(mean_risk, 1)) %>%
  kable(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = FALSE, linesep = rep("", 5), caption = "K-means cluster profile (k = 6).") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 8.5)
```

K-means (`nstart = 25`) was run on latitude and longitude converted to 3-D coordinates on the globe (so longitude wraps correctly), log depth and magnitude, all standardised. The clusters differ mainly by depth and magnitude: cluster `r cl$cluster[which.max(cl$mean_depth)]` holds the deep events (mean depth `r round(max(cl$mean_depth))` km, lowest risk), cluster `r cl$cluster[which.max(cl$mean_mag)]` the largest events (mean magnitude `r f2(max(cl$mean_mag))`, highest risk) and cluster `r cl$cluster[which.min(cl$mean_depth)]` the shallowest. **Caution:** the elbow plot has no sharp bend and the silhouette width is highest at k = 2 (about 0.32, against 0.25 at k = 6), so k = 6 is a descriptive choice, not a strongly supported one.

# Prediction model

**Task.** Classify an event as **High/Severe** (the positive class, `r pct(mean(eq$risk_level %in% c("High","Severe")))` of events) or Low/Moderate. **Why these methods.** Logistic regression is a simple, interpretable baseline; a decision tree gives readable rules; a random forest combines many trees and can capture non-linear interactions between location and time, so it is a natural candidate when location drives the pattern. All three are compared on the same held-out test set. Magnitude and depth are **excluded** from the inputs because they define the risk score (using them would be data leakage); the inputs are latitude, longitude, year, month, hour, review status and magnitude type.

\Needspace{20\baselineskip}

```{r model-code, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
# Abbreviated from earthquake_analysis.R (Phases 8B and 9); not re-run here so that the
# results below are exactly the ones saved in outputs/tables/model_comparison.csv
model_df <- eq %>% transmute(
  high_risk = factor(ifelse(risk_level %in% c("High", "Severe"), "High", "NotHigh"),
                     levels = c("High", "NotHigh")),
  latitude, longitude, year, month, hour, status_code, magnitude_type)
idx   <- caret::createDataPartition(model_df$high_risk, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)  # stratified 80/20
train <- model_df[idx, ];  test <- model_df[-idx, ]
glm_fit  <- glm(high_risk ~ ., data = train, family = binomial)
tree_fit <- rpart::rpart(high_risk ~ ., data = train, method = "class", cp = 0.005)
rf_fit   <- randomForest::randomForest(high_risk ~ ., data = train, ntree = 300, importance = TRUE)
# accuracy, precision, recall, F1: caret::confusionMatrix();  AUC and ROC: pROC::roc()
```

```{r cmp}
cmp <- read_csv(P("outputs", "tables", "model_comparison.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
imp <- read_csv(P("outputs", "tables", "feature_importance.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
best <- cmp %>% arrange(desc(f1), desc(auc)) %>% slice(1)
base_acc <- mean(!(eq$risk_level %in% c("High", "Severe")))
cmp %>% mutate(across(-model, ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  rename(Model = model, Accuracy = accuracy, Precision = precision, Recall = recall, F1 = f1, AUC = auc) %>%
  kable(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = FALSE, linesep = rep("", 5),
        caption = "Test-set results (positive class = High/Severe; about 4,650 test earthquakes).") %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 8.5)
```

```{r f-roc, results = "asis"}
two_fig(fig("62_roc_curves.png"), fig("65_feature_importance.png"),
        "ROC curves of the three models (left) and random forest feature importance (right).")
```

# Results

The **random forest is the best model on every measure**: accuracy `r f3(best$accuracy)`, precision `r f3(best$precision)`, recall `r f3(best$recall)`, F1 `r f3(best$f1)` and AUC `r f3(best$auc)`. Logistic regression and the decision tree barely beat a model that always predicts "not High/Severe" (accuracy `r f3(base_acc)`) and find only about 11% of High/Severe events (recall `r f2(cmp$recall[1])` and `r f2(cmp$recall[2])`); the random forest finds about `r pct(best$recall, 0)`. Its ROC curve lies above the others (AUC `r f2(best$auc)`), a moderate ability to rank High/Severe events higher than others. Longitude and latitude are the most important inputs, which reflects the concentration of severe events along particular plate boundaries; `year` and `magnitude_type` are also important, but they describe how an event was catalogued and act partly as proxies for magnitude, so the model should not be read as finding physical causes.

# Conclusion

From `r format(nrow(raw), big.mark = ",")` raw records, `r format(nrow(eq), big.mark = ",")` natural earthquakes were analysed. Most are shallow (`r pct(mean(eq$depth < 70))` above 70 km) and lie along plate boundaries, and the explainable risk score places `r pct(mean(eq$risk_level %in% c("High", "Severe")))` of them in the High or Severe levels. A random forest recognised these events better than logistic regression or a decision tree (F1 `r f2(best$f1)`, AUC `r f2(best$auc)`), but only moderately better than a trivial baseline.

**Limitations.** The risk score uses author-chosen weights (60/40) and ignores exposure; the catalogue is limited to magnitude 5.5 and above; k = 6 is weakly supported; and model skill is modest. Random steps (train/test split, clustering) depend on the random-number stream: re-running the pipeline in another R environment reproduced the cleaning, risk-level counts and model ranking, but not the exact metrics, and the decision tree collapsed to a single node. Cross-validation would give more stable figures. An interactive Shiny dashboard (`app.R`) and an extended 21-page report (`report/earthquake_report_extended.pdf`) are in the repository.
